# SURAKSHA Connection Guide: Data → GEE → Flood Pipeline → API → App

This guide explains how to connect the components in this repository into a working service. Implement one narrow path at a time. Keep every input's source and quality attached to its output so a demo, fallback, or model estimate cannot be mistaken for an observation.

Related roadmap: [GEE, API, and application integration plan](/docs?doc=06-geospatial-intelligence--gee-api-application-integration-plan). Repository state used: commit `d34347f`.

## 1. Target architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CWC[CWC / WRD observations] --> ING[Provider adapters + time series]
  IMD[IMD rainfall] --> ING
  EE[GEE service] --> S1[Sentinel-1 flood extent]
  EE --> S2[Sentinel-2 snow / snowline]
  EE --> SNOW[S1 wet-snow observations]
  ING --> WF[One production flood workflow]
  S1 --> WF
  S2 --> WF
  SNOW --> MELT[Calibrated melt + basin routing]
  MELT --> WF
  WF --> EXP[Hydraulic forecast + exposure + lifecycle gates]
  EXP --> API[Authenticated FastAPI + job store]
  API --> WEB[Website / future mobile app]
```

The website/mobile client talks only to SURAKSHA's HTTPS API. The SURAKSHA server talks to GEE and hydrological providers. GEE credentials never go into a browser or mobile bundle. The API credential is a separate credential and should also remain server-side for browser use; use user authentication or a website backend-for-frontend.

## 2. Prepare credentials, providers, and dependencies

1. Create/select and register a Google Cloud project for Earth Engine, enable the Earth Engine API, and confirm your user/service identity has access. Google requires a Cloud project for Python client initialization. See the [authentication guide](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/auth) and [service account guide](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/service_account).
2. Install the project with GEE support and configure `EE_PROJECT_ID` in `.env`:

   ```powershell
   python -m pip install -e ".[geo,api]"
   if (-not (Test-Path .env)) { Copy-Item .env.example .env }
   # Edit .env and set EE_PROJECT_ID to the Cloud project ID
   python scripts/setup_earth_engine.py --authenticate
   ```

   The setup command authenticates the local user when requested, initializes the client, and makes a small server round-trip. You can pass `--project YOUR_PROJECT_ID` instead of setting `EE_PROJECT_ID`. Do not replace an existing `.env` file with the example.
3. For an unattended deployment, use Application Default Credentials/workload identity from the hosting platform. A service-account key file is supported for environments that cannot use ADC by setting `EE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_KEY_FILE`; keep it outside source control and never place it in a browser/mobile bundle. See Google's guidance on [ADC for unattended access](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/service_account#authenticate-to-earth-engine-using-application-default-credentials).
4. Keep project IDs and credential configuration in deployment configuration/secrets. Never commit service-account JSON. Never return private credential paths or provider error strings that may contain sensitive details in public health responses.
5. Establish access and refresh rules for CWC/WRD stage/discharge and IMD rainfall. Confirm the station IDs, datum, units, timestamp timezone, licensing, and rate limits before writing adapters. Do not assume Earth Engine supplies these hydrology feeds.
6. Define configuration names for provider endpoints, project ID, timeouts, cache/job storage, CORS origins, and auth issuer. Validate required configuration at startup and expose only safe status fields.

Local interactive Earth Engine initialization follows the documented `ee.Authenticate()` then `ee.Initialize(project=...)` flow. Do not use this interactive flow as the hosted service's credential mechanism. See Google's [Python quickstart](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/quickstart_python) and [unattended auth guidance](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/service_account).

## 3. Define shared observation and product contracts

Create typed Pydantic contracts in `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/contracts/` before wiring providers. At minimum represent:

```python
class ObservationProvenance(BaseModel):
    source: str
    observed_at: datetime | None
    ingested_at: datetime
    quality: Literal["verified", "provisional", "degraded", "missing"]
    is_fallback: bool = False
    source_record_id: str | None = None
    notes: list[str] = []

class TimedValue(BaseModel):
    value: float | None
    unit: str
    provenance: ObservationProvenance
```

Use immutable, timezone-aware records. Add AOI/CRS and acquisition windows to satellite products; add model/version, valid time, lead time, and uncertainty to forecasts. Use `None` plus a reason for missing measurements. Avoid filling unknown values with physical-looking defaults. Track an explicit `mode` such as `live`, `operator_supplied`, or `demo` on input and output.

Store the canonical four-feature forecast history in the model's required order: `water_level_m`, `rainfall_mm`, `upstream_discharge_cumec`, `soil_moisture_index`. Validate units, order, cadence, gaps, and the full 72-hour history before inference. If it is incomplete, use an explicitly approved fallback or escalate; never silently synthesize the window.

## 4. Build provider adapters first

Keep network I/O outside agents and numerical models. Add provider modules under `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/ingestion/` (or a clearly named providers package), for example:

- `CwcProvider.fetch_observations(station_id, start, end)`
- `ImdProvider.fetch_rainfall(catchment_id, start, end)`
- `GeeProductService.submit(product_request)` and `get_status(task_id)`

Each adapter should return validated contracts, enforce timeouts, handle pagination/rate limits, reject malformed units/timestamps, and map outages to a typed degraded/unavailable result. Keep retry behavior bounded and idempotent. Cache stable results by provider, product, AOI/station, time window, and processor version.

Connect `CatchmentIngestionEngine` to these adapters rather than having each agent make separate ad-hoc requests. The scheduler should accept a provider interface, not `mock_feed` as its only polling path. Keep mock feeds only in tests/demo mode and make their provenance unmistakable.

## 5. Make Earth Engine a reusable processing service

### Initialization

Refactor `EarthEngineClient` to initialize once per process/application lifespan and inject it into processors. It should expose a safe diagnostic result: installed, initialized, project ID, auth mode, and last sanitized error category. Do not mark a provider healthy just because initialization was attempted.

### Implement and validate products

1. **Sentinel-1 flood extent:** query `COPERNICUS/S1_GRD` by AOI, acquisition window, IW mode, polarization, and orbit/pass as required. Confirm the collection is non-empty and enough valid pixels remain. Use a documented and calibrated classification method, permanent-water handling, and optional pre-event reference. Return scene IDs/dates, algorithm version, valid coverage, area, GeoJSON/raster reference, and quality flags. The current fallback polygon must be available only through explicit demo mode.
2. **Sentinel-2 snow cover/snowline:** query the harmonized surface reflectance collection; apply cloud/shadow masks; calculate snow cover/NDSI and elevation-based snowline for valid pixels. Return scene dates, cloud/coverage information, selected tile/AOI, and uncertainty. Do not return tile baseline altitude as an observed snowline.
3. **Sentinel-1 wet snow:** implement matched current/frozen-reference acquisitions with orbit/polarization compatibility and backscatter change thresholds. Return reference/current scene metadata, threshold/method, valid-pixel coverage, wet-snow area, and quality. The current authenticated branch is a stub and should not feed operational melt calculations.
4. **Before/after change detection:** select comparable acquisitions around supplied event dates; calculate flood/damage change only for valid pixels; preserve pre/post scene IDs and masks. Remove forced offline mode only after the real pipeline has honest empty-scene/error behavior.

Start with small, known AOIs and scene windows; compare results with manually reviewed scenes before broadening. Handle no scenes, clouds, partial coverage, permission failure, request timeout, and quota errors explicitly. Earth Engine interactive requests and batch work have different uses; submit large exports as asynchronous tasks and track them. Respect project quotas and limit concurrent work—see Google's [processing environments](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/processing_environments) and [quota guidance](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/guides/usage).

Do not turn a failed EE call into an apparently successful feature collection. For interactive products, return a typed unavailable/degraded result. For large products, persist an EE task ID and result location.

## 6. Connect one complete forecast path

Refactor `FloodPipelineRunner` to receive injected services/adapters; avoid global singleton side effects where they hide configuration. The first end-to-end runtime flow should be:

1. Receive station/catchment and forecast time window.
2. Fetch gauge and rainfall histories; validate the 72-hour feature window and provenance.
3. Request or reuse GEE products for the same AOI/time window where needed.
4. Run DataAgent/WeatherAgent with those typed inputs. Agents validate and transform evidence; they must not invent a substitute observation.
5. If cryosphere evidence is available and validated, pass it with real temperature and calibrated sub-basin melt parameters into the melt model. Route only basin-connected runoff.
6. Route tributary and upstream discharge through the hydraulic corridor model. Record calibration/version and boundary conditions.
7. Run forecasting, risk, inundation, exposure, and the lifecycle gates against the same input snapshot.
8. Return forecasts as estimates and satellite/gauge observations as observations, each with provenance, times, quality, and uncertainty.

Make the plan from Jev executable: inspect `required_agents`, primary route, challenger, and approved fallback; dispatch that route; enforce the deterministic policy's returned action. Write an execution trace for selected and actually executed routes. Do not let a gate that says retry/fallback/escalate simply append metadata and continue as normal.

Use a separate explicit demo path for canned values. Replace `value or default` logic with `value if value is not None else ...` when zero is valid; for operational paths, prefer a validation error or degraded state over a default. Do not stamp the current time onto an old or synthetic value and label it as observed now.

## 7. Connect real inundation to impacts and lifecycle

1. Make the satellite/hydraulic output a GeoJSON polygon or depth raster with a known CRS, time, and resolution.
2. Pass that geometry/raster through `ImpactAgent` into `SpatialExposureEngine`.
3. Intersect WorldPop raster cells and real asset/road vectors with the inundation product. Use depth thresholds where assets/population impacts depend on depth. Handle nodata and CRS reprojection deliberately.
4. Keep density-based estimates only as a named provisional fallback, never label them as a spatial overlay.
5. In POST_EVENT, require actual peak/time evidence, dated pre/post imagery, and independent impact evidence for certification. If evidence is missing or all agents share one source, return provisional/human-review status.

## 8. Expose a safe asynchronous API

Keep route functions thin. Define request/response schemas and typed errors first. Suggested flow:

```text
POST /api/v1/flood/forecast-jobs   -> 202 {job_id, status_url}
GET  /api/v1/jobs/{job_id}         -> queued | running | succeeded | degraded | failed
GET  /api/v1/flood/forecasts/{id}  -> forecast + provenance + uncertainty
POST /api/v1/flood/satellite-jobs -> 202 {job_id, status_url}
GET  /api/v1/health                -> per-provider readiness
GET  /api/v1/flood/stations        -> station metadata
```

Use durable job storage and a worker/queue for expensive GEE and flood runs; API process memory is not durable job state. Add request IDs, idempotency keys, auth/authorization, rate limits, timeouts, audit logs, and result retention. Configure CORS to known web origins only; do not combine wildcard origins with credentialed browser requests. Health should show GEE, CWC/WRD, IMD, storage/queue, model registry, and Jev status separately.

Keep the production API credential server-side. For the website, use user sign-in or a server-side route that calls SURAKSHA. For the future mobile app, use user-scoped tokens stored in OS secure storage and the same API contract. Rotate/revoke credentials and do not log bearer tokens.

## 9. Wire the separate website after the contract exists

The current workspace contains no website/mobile client. First confirm the website repo's current state. Then build UI against the OpenAPI schema, not a second copy of model logic. Initial screens should show station selection, forecast job progress, forecast time series, current observation freshness, satellite acquisition dates, impact map, source/quality labels, and degraded/unavailable states. Never show a synthetic/demo result without a visible demo label.

Do not begin the mobile app until the same API contract has stabilized. Web and mobile can share generated API types/client code from OpenAPI, but each must use its own secure user-auth flow.

## 10. Prove each connection before moving on

Use these acceptance checks as implementation milestones (they are instructions, not claims that they already pass):

1. **Provider adapter:** a dated real record returns the expected units/time/source; outage and malformed responses become unavailable/degraded without defaults.
2. **GEE:** a known AOI produces scene IDs, dates, coverage, and a reproducible product; no-scene/auth failure does not emit a synthetic observation.
3. **Window assembly:** exact four-feature 72-hour window, ordered and timezone-aligned; missing feature blocks or explicitly downgrades inference.
4. **Runtime:** trace shows real input record IDs through agents, chosen Jev route, model, hydraulic route, and output provenance.
5. **Spatial impact:** polygon/depth fixture intersects known raster cells/assets and yields expected counts with CRS documented.
6. **API:** unauthenticated calls are rejected where required; valid clients submit a job, poll it, and retrieve a typed result; provider failures remain visible.
7. **Website:** UI renders live, stale, provisional, demo, degraded, and unavailable status correctly against staging API.
8. **Operational replay:** independent held-out observed flood hydrographs and satellite masks support reported metrics. Separate reanalysis benchmarks from gauge-verified results.

Keep these as a growing CI suite and run the relevant checks after each milestone. Add a staging deployment and provider integration checks before production. A green unit suite alone does not establish scientific validity.

## 11. Suggested implementation order

1. Add truthful provenance contracts and an explicit demo/live distinction; remove fake defaults from production paths.
2. Implement provider adapters and the genuine timestamped input window.
3. Complete GEE flood extent first; add wet-snow, snowline, and post-event change products only after each has validated quality metadata.
4. Connect melt and corridor routing to the main runner; validate against gauge hydrographs.
5. Connect polygon/depth products to exposure and make lifecycle certification evidence-gated.
6. Make Jev runtime routing executable and deterministic gate actions effective.
7. Add authenticated API, durable jobs/storage, deployment, monitoring, and provider health.
8. Build the website against OpenAPI, then the mobile app against that same contract.

The first useful milestone is intentionally small: **real CWC/IMD input → validated forecast → authenticated API job/result → website display with timestamps and provenance**. Add GEE flood extent as the next connected product, then bring cryosphere and POST_EVENT products into the science only after their own validation.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Flood Inundation Processing
summary: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) on board the Copernicus Sentinel-1 constellation operates at C-band (5.405 GHz). Unlike optical sensors (e.g. Sentinel-2, Landsat), SAR microwave pulses penetrate dense ...
content:
# Sentinel-1 SAR Flood Inundation Processing | Field | Value | |---|---| | **Document ID** | GEO-06-001 | | **Version** | 1.0.0 | | **Status** | VERIFIED | | **Module** | SURAKSHA-MOD-01-FLOOD | | **Source Implementation** | `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/geospatial/s1_sar_processor.py` | --- ## 1. Sensor Overview & Physical Principles Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) on board the Copernicus Sentinel-1 constellation operates at C-band (5.405 GHz). Unlike optical sensors (e.g. Sentinel-2, Landsat), SAR microwave pulses penetrate dense monsoon cloud cover and operate independently of solar illumination. ### 1.1 Radar Backscatter Mechanism Smooth, standing water surfaces act as specular reflectors for incoming radar microwave radiation. The signal bounces away from the sensor, resulting in extremely low radar backscatter: $$\sigma^0_{\text{water}} \approx -24\text{ dB to }-16\text{ dB}$$ In contrast, rough bare soil, vegetation, and urban infrastructure generate diffuse scattering or double-bounce returns: $$\sigma^0_{\text{land}} \approx -14\text{ dB to }-6\text{ dB}$$ --- ## 2. Processing Pipeline The SURAKSHA `Sentinel1SARProcessor` implements a 7-step automated processing pipeline: ```mermaid flowchart LR S1[Sentinel-1 GRD
IW / VV Polarization] --> Orbit[Apply Precise
Orbit Vectors] Orbit --> Calib[Radiometric
Calibration σ⁰] Calib --> Terrain[Terrain Correction
SRTM 30m] Terrain --> Lee[Lee Speckle Filter
7x7 Window] Lee --> Otsu[Otsu Automated
Thresholding] Otsu --> PermMask[Subtract JRC
Permanent Water] PermMask --> SlopeMask[Mask Slopes > 5°
SRTM DEM] SlopeMask --> NetFlood[Net Flooded
Acreage Polygon] ``` ### 2.1 Speckle Noise Reduction (Refined Lee Filter) Raw SAR images contain multiplicative speckle noise caused by coherent interference. We apply a $7\times 7$ Refined Lee filter: $$\hat{I} = \bar{I} + W \cdot (I - \bar{I})$$ where the weighting coefficient $W$ is derived from local variance: $$W = \frac{\sigma^2_I - \bar{I}^2 / N}{\sigma^2_I}$$ ### 2.2 Otsu Bimodal Thresholding The processor dynamically computes the optimal bimodal threshold $\tau^*$ separating water and non-water pixels in the VV backscatter histogram by maximizing inter-class variance: $$\sigma^2_B(\tau) = \omega_0(\tau)\omega_1(\tau)[\mu_0(\tau) - \mu_1(\tau)]^2$$ Typical thresholds for the Patna Ganga corridor range between $-17.5\text{ dB}$ and $-16.0\text{ dB}$. ### 2.3 Permanent Water Subtraction & Slope Masking 1. **Permanent Water**: Extracted from JRC Global Surface Water (water occurrence $\ge 80\%$). 2. **Terrain Masking**: Inundation cannot stand on steep slopes. Pixels with SRTM slope $> 5^\circ$ are rejected to eliminate radar shadow false positives. --- ## 3. Offline Calibrated Fallback Mode When Google Earth Engine (GEE) authentication is unavailable or internet connectivity is disrupted: - The system activates `OfflineFallbackSAR`. - Utilizes calibrated historical flood polygon benchmarks for Patna (2016, 2019, 2021) stored as local GeoJSON assets. - Scales the inundation extent linearly based on observed gauge height at Gandhi Ghat: $$A_{\text{inundated}}(h) = A_{\text{base}} \cdot \max\left(0, \frac{h - h_{\text{warning}}}{h_{\text{HFL}} - h_{\text{warning}}}\right)^{1.35}$$

title: Flood Forecasting & Risk Models Architecture

content:
# Flood Forecasting & Risk Models Architecture

## 1. Candidate Forecasting Model Ladder
The SURAKSHA Flood Subsystem treats hydrological time-series prediction not as a sequential pipeline of models, but as an empirical **candidate pool** benchmarked under identical conditions on historical gauge telemetry and Copernicus atmospheric data.

All forecasting models conform to `BaseFloodForecaster` (`src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/base.py`):
- **Input**: Lookback window of shape `(L=72 hours, F=4 features)`:
  - `water_level_m`
  - `precipitation`
  - `river_discharge_m3s`
  - `soil_moisture_0_to_7cm`
- **Output**: Multi-horizon projections:
  - `t_plus_6`: +6 hours water stage (m)
  - `t_plus_12`: +12 hours water stage (m)
  - `t_plus_24`: +24 hours water stage (m)

---

### Candidate 1: Persistence Forecaster (`persistence.py`)
* **Mathematical Baseline**: $\hat{y}_{t+h} = y_t$
* **Purpose**: Fundamental zero-skill benchmark against which all statistical and deep learning models are evaluated.

### Candidate 2: ARIMA (`arima_sarima.py`)
* **Specification**: $\text{ARIMA}(2, 1, 1)$ Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average.
* **Mechanism**: Models autocorrelation in hydrological rate-of-rise $\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$.
* **Execution**: Fitted on historical series; applied out-of-sample via statespace filtering.

### Candidate 3: SARIMA (`arima_sarima.py`)
* **Specification**: $\text{SARIMA}(1, 1, 1) \times (1, 0, 1)_{24}$ Seasonal ARIMA.
* **Mechanism**: Captures 24-hour diurnal monsoon rainfall cycles and solar evapotranspiration fluctuations.

### Candidate 4: GRU Forecaster (`gru.py`)
* **Specification**: 2-layer Gated Recurrent Unit (`hidden_size=64`, `dropout=0.15`).
* **Mechanism**: Efficient gated recurrence with lower parameter footprint, ideal for rapid edge updates on remote river monitoring nodes.

### Candidate 5: Causal Multi-Horizon LSTM (`causal_lstm.py`)
* **Specification**: 2-layer Causal Long Short-Term Memory network (`hidden_size=64`, `dropout=0.20`).
* **Multi-Horizon Head**: Separate linear projection heads for +6h, +12h, and +24h lead times. Strictly causal past lookback without lookahead leakage.

### Candidate 6: Hybrid BiLSTM Forecaster (`bilstm_hybrid.py`)
* **Specification**: Bidirectional LSTM encoder across the 72-hour historical window + 1D Temporal Convolutional residual feature extractor + Multi-horizon decoder.
* **Mechanism**: Captures sudden upstream flash-flood surges and antecedent basin saturation simultaneously.

---

## 2. Benchmark Ladder Evaluator (`benchmark_ladder.py`)
The `ForecastLadderBenchmark` orchestrates parallel training and validation across the 6 candidate models on identical test sequences.
* **Evaluation Metrics**:
  - Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) at 24h
  - Mean Absolute Error (MAE) at 24h
  - Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) at 24h:
    $$NSE = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2}{\sum (y_t - \bar{y})^2}$$
* **Production Selection**: The candidate achieving the highest Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency is automatically selected and registered into `ForecastAgent`.

---

## 3. Calibrated Risk Model (`src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/risk/risk_model.py`)
Independent from the hydrological stage forecasting ladder, SURAKSHA employs a dedicated **Calibrated Risk Model** (XGBoost / Gradient Boosting) to translate physical stage heights and spatial vulnerability into operational disaster risk.

### Features Ingested:
1. `forecast_stage_24h`
2. `danger_level_m`
3. `stage_to_danger_ratio` ($y_{t+24} / y_{\text{danger}}$)
4. `rate_of_rise_m_per_hr`
5. `precipitation_24h_mm`
6. `antecedent_precipitation_3d` ($API_{3d}$)
7. `antecedent_precipitation_7d` ($API_{7d}$)
8. `soil_moisture_level`
9. `district_vulnerability_index`

### Model Outputs:
* `risk_score`: Continuous probability calibrated to $[0.0, 1.0]$.
* `severity`: Categorical classification (`LOW`, `MODERATE`, `HIGH`, `CRITICAL`).
* `threshold_breach_expected`: Boolean indicating expected breach of danger or warning stage.
* `drivers`: Top 3 contributing features ordered by feature importance.

# Flood Forecasting Model Ladder: Empirical Evaluation & Benchmarks

## 1. Executive Summary & Benchmark Framework
In accordance with the SURAKSHA scientific architecture, forecasting models do not form a sequential inference chain. Instead, they constitute an **empirical candidate pool** evaluated under identical retrospective sequences ($L=72\text{h}$ lookback, $H=24\text{h}$ horizon) on authentic hourly hydrological telemetry from Copernicus GloFAS and ERA5-Land reanalysis for the Ganges at Patna.

The candidate pool spans baseline persistence, classical statistical time-series models, and modern deep recurrent architectures:
1. **Persistence Forecaster** (Zero-skill mathematical baseline)
2. **ARIMA(2, 1, 1)** (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average)
3. **SARIMA(1, 1, 1)x(1, 0, 1, 24)** (Seasonal ARIMA with diurnal cycle)
4. **GRU** (2-layer Gated Recurrent Unit)
5. **Causal LSTM** (2-layer Causal Long Short-Term Memory)
6. **Hybrid BiLSTM** (Bidirectional LSTM encoder + Temporal CNN residual filter)

---

## 2. Empirical Benchmark Results (Ganges at Patna Station)

Evaluated across the held-out test split of the authentic Copernicus hourly hydrological timeseries:

| Candidate Model | 24h RMSE (m) | 24h MAE (m) | Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency ($NSE_{24\text{h}}$) | Status / Operational Role |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **SARIMA(1, 1, 1)x(1, 0, 1, 24)** | **0.181** | **0.092** | **0.981** | **Top Statistical Winner (Diurnal Cycle)** |
| **Persistence ($y_{t+h} = y_t$)** | 0.183 | 0.155 | 0.980 | Baseline Benchmark |
| **ARIMA(2, 1, 1)** | 0.183 | 0.155 | 0.980 | Momentum Benchmark |
| **Hybrid BiLSTM (Research)** | **0.225** | **0.200** | **0.970** | **Top Deep Learning Winner (Multi-Feature Exogenous)** |
| **Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)** | 0.278 | 0.250 | 0.954 | Lightweight Recurrent Edge Candidate |
| **Causal LSTM** | 0.417 | 0.366 | 0.897 | Standard Deep Recurrent Baseline |

---

## 3. Scientific Insights & Operational Conclusions

1. **Diurnal Seasonality Importance**:
   - In low-gradient river plains like the lower Ganges basin during non-monsoon periods, river levels exhibit marked diurnal variations due to upstream dam releases and evapotranspiration. SARIMA's 24-hour seasonal lag enables it to achieve an extraordinary **MAE of 0.092m** and **NSE of 0.981**.
2. **Multi-Feature Exogenous Power (Hybrid BiLSTM)**:
   - While statistical models track immediate rate-of-rise autocorrelation, **Hybrid BiLSTM** explicitly ingests catchment precipitation, GloFAS discharge, and root-zone soil moisture ($0 → 7\text{cm}$), making it the premier architecture for anticipating sudden upstream storm surges prior to physical arrival at the gauge.
3. **Decoupled Risk Layer**:
   - As designed, physical forecasting is strictly insulated from risk calculation. Regardless of which forecaster is chosen by the ladder benchmark, its multi-horizon stage estimates ($t+6, t+12, t+24\text{h}$) feed directly into the calibrated **Risk Model (XGBoost / Gradient Boosting)** and the **TypeSafe Jev System One** verification layer.

title: Forecasting Methodology: Champion-Challenger Model Ladder

content:
# Forecasting Methodology: Champion-Challenger Model Ladder

<!-- Status: VERIFIED — content derived from /src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/ -->

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Category** | 07 — AI & Machine Learning |
| **Status** | VERIFIED |
| **Last Updated** | 2026-11-21 |
| **Maintainer** | SURAKSHA Flood Subsystem Team |
| **Source files** | `/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/` |

---

## 1. Motivation: Why a Ladder Architecture?

A single-model production system exhibits three critical failure modes in the hydrological domain:

1. **Distribution shift fragility**: A model trained on past monsoon seasons may perform poorly during unprecedented precipitation events outside its training distribution.
2. **Cold-start failures**: Statistical models require sufficient fitted history; neural models need loaded checkpoint weights. A single model that fails to load leaves the pipeline blind.
3. **No reference baseline**: Without a naive baseline, there is no way to determine whether a model is adding value or degrading predictions.

The **champion-challenger ladder** addresses all three failure modes:
- Every candidate is benchmarked under identical conditions.
- The highest-NSE candidate becomes the **production champion**.
- Each champion has an explicit **fallback chain** to the next-best model.
- The naive **Persistence baseline** serves as the irreducible minimum benchmark.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The ladder benchmark is an *offline* process that selects the champion. At runtime, the production champion executes; it only degrades to its fallback if its checkpoint is unavailable or prediction raises an exception.

---

## 2. Candidate Pool

The ladder evaluates **6 candidates** in ascending order of model complexity:

| # | Model | Class | Framework | Architecture |
|---|-------|-------|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | **Persistence** | Baseline | NumPy | y(t+H) = y(t) |
| 2 | **ARIMA(2,1,1)** | Statistical | statsmodels | Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average |
| 3 | **SARIMA(1,1,1)×(1,0,1)₂₄** | Statistical | statsmodels SARIMAX | Seasonal ARIMA with 24h diurnal seasonality |
| 4 | **GRU-2layer-h32** | Deep Learning | PyTorch | Gated Recurrent Unit, 2 layers, hidden_dim=32 |
| 5 | **Causal LSTM-2layer-h32** | Deep Learning | PyTorch | Unidirectional LSTM, 2 layers, hidden_dim=32 |
| 6 | **Hybrid BiLSTM+1DCNN** | Deep Learning (Research) | PyTorch | Bidirectional LSTM + 1D Temporal CNN |

> [!NOTE]
> The hidden dimension in the production checkpoints is **32** (not 64), as found in the actual model instantiation: `HydrologicalGRUModel(input_dim=4, hidden_dim=32, num_layers=2)`. The briefing description of "h64" is a documentation approximation; the verified code uses `hidden_dim=32`.

### Source files
- Persistence: [`/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/persistence.py`](https://github.com/shouri123/SURAKSHA/tree/main/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/persistence.py)
- ARIMA & SARIMA: [`/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/arima_sarima.py`](https://github.com/shouri123/SURAKSHA/tree/main/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/arima_sarima.py)
- GRU: [`/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/gru.py`](https://github.com/shouri123/SURAKSHA/tree/main/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/gru.py)
- Causal LSTM: [`/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/causal_lstm.py`](https://github.com/shouri123/SURAKSHA/tree/main/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/causal_lstm.py)
- Hybrid BiLSTM: [`/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/bilstm_hybrid.py`](https://github.com/shouri123/SURAKSHA/tree/main/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/bilstm_hybrid.py)
- Benchmark runner: [`/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/benchmark_ladder.py`](https://github.com/shouri123/SURAKSHA/tree/main/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/benchmark_ladder.py)

---

## 3. Input Feature Specification

All deep learning candidates and the statistical models share the same **input lookback window**:

```
X ∈ ℝ^(72 × 4)   — 72-hour lookback window × 4 input features
```

| Index | Feature | Unit | Physical meaning |
|-------|---------|------|-----------------|
| 0 | `water_level_m` | m MSL | Observed river stage height at CWC Gandhi Ghat gauge |
| 1 | `precipitation` | mm/hr | Catchment-averaged hourly precipitation |
| 2 | `river_discharge_m3s` | m³/s | River discharge rate from upstream gauges |
| 3 | `soil_moisture_0_to_7cm` | m³/m³ | ERA5-Land surface soil moisture (0–7 cm depth) |

**Output specification:**

```
ŷ ∈ {t+6h, t+12h, t+24h}   — predicted stage height in metres MSL
```

Three separate scalar predictions are issued for the 6-hour, 12-hour, and 24-hour forecast horizons.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The lookback window is **strictly historical** — the model only observes past data up to and including the current timestep t. No future observations or concurrent targets are included in the input tensor. This causal integrity applies equally to all candidates including the BiLSTM.

---

## 4. Model Descriptions and Mathematical Formulations

### 4.1 Candidate 1: Persistence Baseline

The simplest possible forecast: the river stage at all future horizons equals its current value.

$$\hat{y}(t+H) = y(t) \quad \forall H \in \{6, 12, 24\}$$

**Purpose**: The persistence baseline is the minimum benchmark that any model must beat. If a sophisticated model cannot outperform persistence, it provides no operational value. All ladder candidates must achieve a higher NSE than persistence.

**Fallback**: This is the terminal fallback — it always succeeds and requires no fitting.

---

### 4.2 Candidate 2: ARIMA(2,1,1)

**ARIMA** (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average) models the differenced time series as a function of its own lagged values and lagged forecast errors.

**Model specification**: ARIMA(p=2, d=1, q=1) with `trend="t"` (linear drift)

The general ARIMA(p,d,q) model for the d-th differenced series $\Delta^d y_t$:

$$\phi(B) \Delta^d y_t = \theta(B) \varepsilon_t$$

Where:
- $B$ is the backshift operator: $B y_t = y_{t-1}$
- $\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \phi_2 B^2$ (AR polynomial, p=2)
- $\theta(B) = 1 + \theta_1 B$ (MA polynomial, q=1)
- $\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$ (first difference, d=1)
- $\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ is white noise

**Training details**:
- Fit on the trailing **500 hours** of training series (sliding window for stability)
- Implemented via `statsmodels.tsa.arima.model.ARIMA`

**Rain-surge proportional scaling** applied post-prediction:

```
rain_surge = min(1.20, mean_rain_12h × 0.008)
ŷ(t+6)  += rain_surge × 0.35
ŷ(t+12) += rain_surge × 0.65
ŷ(t+24) += rain_surge × 1.00
```

**Autoregressive momentum fallback** (when fitted model unavailable):

```
δ = y(t) - y(t-6)   # 6-hour momentum
ŷ(t+6)  = y(t) + 0.25δ + rain_surge × 0.35
ŷ(t+12) = y(t) + 0.50δ + rain_surge × 0.65
ŷ(t+24) = y(t) + 0.80δ + rain_surge × 1.00
```

**Physical output clamping**: $\hat{y}(t+H) \in [0.0\text{ m},\ 55.0\text{ m MSL}]$

---

### 4.3 Candidate 3: SARIMA(1,1,1)×(1,0,1)₂₄

**SARIMA** (Seasonal ARIMA) extends ARIMA with a seasonal component that captures the **24-hour diurnal cycle** of monsoon rainfall and evapotranspiration.

**Model specification**: SARIMA(1,1,1)×(1,0,1)₂₄ with `trend="c"` (constant drift)

The SARIMA model combines non-seasonal and seasonal polynomials:

$$\Phi(B^s) \phi(B) \Delta^D_s \Delta^d y_t = \Theta(B^s) \theta(B) \varepsilon_t$$

Where:
- $s = 24$ (seasonal period: 24 hours)
- $\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B$ (non-seasonal AR, p=1)
- $\theta(B) = 1 + \theta_1 B$ (non-seasonal MA, q=1)
- $\Phi(B^{24}) = 1 - \Phi_1 B^{24}$ (seasonal AR, P=1)
- $\Theta(B^{24}) = 1 + \Theta_1 B^{24}$ (seasonal MA, Q=1)
- $\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$ (d=1 differencing)
- $D = 0$ (no seasonal differencing)

**Training details**:
- Fit on trailing **300 hours** (memory-efficient fit window)
- `enforce_stationarity=False`, `maxiter=20`
- Implemented via `statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax.SARIMAX`

**Seasonal lag estimation fallback**:

```
lag_24h_diff = y(t) - y(t-25)
ŷ(t+6)  = y(t) + 0.15 × lag_24h_diff + rain_surge × 0.35
ŷ(t+12) = y(t) + 0.35 × lag_24h_diff + rain_surge × 0.65
ŷ(t+24) = y(t) + 0.60 × lag_24h_diff + rain_surge × 1.00
```

**Physical output clamping**: $\hat{y}(t+H) \in [0.0\text{ m},\ 55.0\text{ m MSL}]$

---

### 4.4 Candidate 4: GRU-2layer-h32

A **Gated Recurrent Unit** (GRU) network that processes the full 72-hour multivariate lookback window sequentially.

**Architecture**:
```
Input  → GRU(input_dim=4, hidden_dim=32, num_layers=2, batch_first=True)
       → FC(hidden_dim=32, out_dim=3)
Output → [ŷ(t+6), ŷ(t+12), ŷ(t+24)]
```

**GRU update equations** at timestep t:

$$z_t = \sigma(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z)$$
$$r_t = \sigma(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t-1} + b_r)$$
$$\tilde{h}_t = \tanh(W_h x_t + U_h (r_t \odot h_{t-1}) + b_h)$$
$$h_t = (1 - z_t) \odot h_{t-1} + z_t \odot \tilde{h}_t$$

Where $z_t$ is the update gate, $r_t$ is the reset gate, $\sigma$ is sigmoid.

**Training**:
- Optimizer: Adam (lr=0.01)
- Loss: MSE
- Epochs: 6, batch_size=128
- Z-score normalization: $(X - \mu) / (\sigma + 10^{-6})$
- Output rescaled: $\hat{y} = \hat{y}_{norm} \times \sigma_y + \mu_y$

---

### 4.5 Candidate 5: Causal LSTM-2layer-h32

A **unidirectional LSTM** (Long Short-Term Memory) with strict causal masking — no information from future timesteps is ever accessed.

**Architecture**:
```
Input  → LSTM(input_dim=4, hidden_dim=32, num_layers=2, batch_first=True)
       → FC(hidden_dim=32, out_dim=3)
Output → [ŷ(t+6), ŷ(t+12), ŷ(t+24)]
```

**LSTM equations** at timestep t:

$$f_t = \sigma(W_f [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_f)$$
$$i_t = \sigma(W_i [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_i)$$
$$\tilde{C}_t = \tanh(W_C [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_C)$$
$$C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t$$
$$o_t = \sigma(W_o [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_o)$$
$$h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t)$$

Where $f_t$, $i_t$, $o_t$ are forget, input, and output gates; $C_t$ is the cell state.

**Training**: Same as GRU (Adam, MSE, 8 epochs, z-score normalization/rescaling).

**Causal integrity**: Only the hidden state at the **final timestep** t (i.e., `out[:, -1, :]`) is passed to the linear decoder head. The model never accesses t+1 through t+24 during inference.

---

### 4.6 Candidate 6: Hybrid BiLSTM+1DCNN (Research)

An advanced research candidate combining a **bidirectional LSTM encoder** with a **1D temporal CNN** residual stream and a **causal multi-horizon decoder**.

**Architecture**:
```
Input (72×4) ──────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
                   │ BiLSTM(4→32, num_layers=2, bidirectional=True)     │ 
                   │ → lstm_out[:, -1, :] ∈ ℝ^64                       │
                   │                                                     │
                   └─ Conv1d(4→64, kernel=3, pad=1) + ReLU              │
                      → conv_out[:, -1, :] ∈ ℝ^64                      │
                                                                        │
Cat([lstm_out, conv_out]) ∈ ℝ^128 ──→ FC(128→3) ──→ [t+6, t+12, t+24] │
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **BiLSTM causal integrity**: The bidirectionality operates **within the historical lookback window only** (t-72 to t). The forward pass reads the 72-hour window left-to-right; the backward pass reads it right-to-left. Neither direction crosses the **prediction boundary at t**. No future observations are included in the input. The decoder outputs are **causally valid** forward predictions.

**Training**: Adam, MSE, 8 epochs, batch_size=128.

**Status**: Labeled `"Hybrid BiLSTM (Research)"` — experimental, pending real-time exogenous validation.

---

## 5. Benchmark Evaluation and Champion Selection

### 5.1 Evaluation Protocol

```python
# ForecastLadderBenchmark.run_benchmark()
# Source: /src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/benchmark_ladder.py

for model in [Persistence, ARIMA, SARIMA, GRU, CausalLSTM, HybridBiLSTM]:
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    metrics = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test_24h)
    # Reports: rmse_24h, mae_24h, nse_24h

df_results = sort_by(nse_24h, descending=True)
winner = df_results.iloc[0]  # Highest NSE becomes production champion
```

### 5.2 Selection Criterion: Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE)

The **Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency** is the primary model selection criterion because it measures skill relative to the climatological mean — a model with NSE=0 is no better than the mean, while NSE=1 is a perfect forecast.

$$\text{NSE} = 1 - \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} (y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2}{\sum_{t=1}^{T} (y_t - \bar{y})^2}$$

Where:
- $y_t$ is the observed stage at time t
- $\hat{y}_t$ is the predicted stage at time t
- $\bar{y}$ is the mean observed stage over the evaluation period
- NSE ∈ (-∞, 1], where NSE=1 is perfect, NSE=0 equals mean-flow prediction, NSE<0 is worse than mean

**Interpretation thresholds** (WMO hydrological model performance):

| NSE Range | Interpretation |
|-----------|---------------|
| > 0.75 | Very good |
| 0.65–0.75 | Good |
| 0.50–0.65 | Satisfactory |
| < 0.50 | Unsatisfactory |

### 5.3 Supplementary Metrics

The benchmark also computes:

| Metric | Formula | Unit |
|--------|---------|------|
| **MAE** | $\frac{1}{T}\sum \|y_t - \hat{y}_t\|$ | m |
| **RMSE** | $\sqrt{\frac{1}{T}\sum (y_t - \hat{y}_t)^2}$ | m |

---

## 6. Fallback Chain

The runtime fallback chain ensures the pipeline never fails to produce a forecast:

```
Production Champion (highest NSE)
    │
    ├─ Checkpoint unavailable / prediction fails?
    │
    ▼
Hybrid BiLSTM+1DCNN
    │
    ▼
GRU-2layer-h32
    │
    ▼
SARIMA(1,1,1)×(1,0,1)₂₄
    │
    ▼
ARIMA(2,1,1)
    │
    ▼
Persistence  ← Always succeeds; terminal fallback
```

> [!WARNING]
> Each fallback step degrades forecast quality. When the pipeline falls back to **Persistence**, the `forecast_confidence` field in `ForecastMultiHorizonState` is set to `"LOW"` and the execution status becomes `"PERSISTENCE_BASELINE_FALLBACK"`. All downstream agents receive this degraded confidence signal.

Fallback triggering conditions (from `ForecastAgent`):
- `fitted_model is None` → `fallback_reason = "fitted_statistical_state_missing"`
- `model is None or not checkpoint_state_loaded` → `fallback_reason = "trained_network_weights_missing"`
- `is_trained == False` → `fallback_reason = "checkpoint_not_marked_trained"`
- Prediction raises exception → `fallback_reason = "prediction_failed:<ExceptionType>"`

---

## 7. Checkpoint Registry

Production checkpoints are stored at:

```
/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/checkpoints/
├── arima_checkpoint.pkl
├── causal_lstm_checkpoint.pkl
├── gru_checkpoint.pkl
├── hybrid_bilstm_(research)_checkpoint.pkl
├── persistence_checkpoint.pkl
├── risk_classifier_calibrated.pkl
├── sarima_checkpoint.pkl
└── registry_metadata.json
```

The checkpoint registry (`registry_metadata.json`) records which model is the active production champion and its benchmark metadata.

---

## 8. Runtime Model Routing

At runtime, the **MidRunGate** routes to different models based on the **data regime** classified at the Pre-Run Gate:

| Data Regime | Strategy | Models Executed |
|------------|---------|----------------|
| `NORMAL` | `SARIMA` | 1 (SARIMA only) |
| `RAPID_RISE` | `ENSEMBLE` | 3 (SARIMA + GRU + Causal LSTM committee) |
| `EXTREME_RAINFALL` | `ENSEMBLE` | 3 (committee) |
| `SENSOR_CONFLICT` | `ENSEMBLE` | 3 (committee, with heightened scrutiny) |
| `MISSING_DATA` | `FALLBACK` | 1 (ARIMA or Persistence) |
| `SATELLITE_UNAVAILABLE` | `SARIMA` | 1 |

The **ForecastCommitteeVerdict** in `SupervisorState` records all committee predictions and the spread adjudication.

---

## 9. Training Dataset

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| **Dataset** | ERA5-Land/GloFAS hourly reanalysis, Open-Meteo Historical API |
| **Period** | May–October 2024 (peak monsoon season) |
| **Duration** | 4,416 hours per station |
| **Gauge** | CWC Gandhi Ghat, Patna (023-MDGANG) |
| **Target** | 24-hour lead water level (m MSL) |
| **Train/Test split** | Chronological (no data leakage) |

> [!CAUTION]
> The training dataset is **ERA5-Land reanalysis** (not live CWC gauge observations). Reanalysis data is modelled/assimilated, not purely measured. NSE scores computed on reanalysis-derived test sets are **not** equivalent to validation on independently observed gauge data. All benchmark results carry this important caveat.

Hidden Dim 32, Dropout 0.2"] Concat["Bidirectional Concatenation [Batch, 64]"] FC["Linear Head [64 → 1]
+ Physical Output Denormalizer"] Output["Forecast Stage y(t+24h) [meters MSL]"] Input --> Conv1D Conv1D --> BiLSTM BiLSTM --> Concat Concat --> FC FC --> Output ``` --- ## 3. Operational Role In the **Mid-Run Gate**, this model acts as the primary challenger to SARIMA during `RAPID_RISE` regimes: - If $|y_{\text{SARIMA}} - y_{\text{BiLSTM}}| \le 0.40\text{ m}$, the ensemble confidence is maximized. - If spread exceeds $0.40\text{ m}$, the supervisor engages TypeSafe Jev System One for committee adjudication.

# Model Card: SARIMA Production Champion

| Field | Value |

| **Model ID** | `SARIMA_111_101_24` |
| **Framework** | `statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax.SARIMAX` |
| **Version** | 2.1.0 (with drift trend and runoff scaling) |
| **Status** | PRODUCTION CHAMPION |
| **Checkpoint** | `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/checkpoints/sarima_checkpoint.pkl` |

---

## 1. Model Summary

A Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA) model with 24-hour diurnal seasonality, constant drift, and proportional rainfall runoff scaling, calibrated for river stage forecasting at Gandhi Ghat, Patna.

$$ARIMA(p=1, d=1, q=1) \times (P=1, D=0, Q=1)_{s=24}$$

---

## 2. Mathematical Formulation

$$\Phi_P(B^{24}) \phi_p(B) (1 - B)^d (y_t - c) = \Theta_Q(B^{24}) \theta_q(B) \epsilon_t + \beta \cdot R_t$$
where:
- $B$ is the backshift operator ($B^k y_t = y_{t-k}$)
- $s = 24$ captures diurnal hydrometeorological cycles
- $c$ is the drift trend parameter (`trend="c"`)
- $R_t$ is the antecedent precipitation runoff surge term
- $\epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ is Gaussian white noise

---

## 3. Training & Validation

- **Training Data**: 8,832 hourly observations (`real_hourly_hydrological_timeseries.csv`), May–October 2024.
- **Physical Clamping**: Forecast stage strictly bounded within $[0.0, 55.0]$ meters MSL.
- **Performance**:
  - **RMSE**: $0.38\text{ m}$
  - **MAE**: $0.29\text{ m}$
  - **Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE)**: $0.91$
  - **Inference Latency**: $8.4\text{ ms}$ on CPU

# Technical Evaluation Report: LSTM vs. BiLSTM Architecture Selection for Hydrological Forecasting & Urban Flood Intelligence **Project**: SURAKSHA (Disaster Intelligence Platform) **Author**: Lead AI/ML Systems Engineer **Date**: September 2026 **Scope**: Flood Subsystem — Sequence Modeling, Regional Tabular Priors & 1D-2D Urban Hydrodynamics --- ## Executive Summary This report delivers the technical and operational blueprint for model selection in the **SURAKSHA Flood Intelligence Subsystem**. It reconciles deep learning sequence architectures (**Unidirectional LSTM** versus **Bidirectional LSTM**) against the empirical reality of all datasets present in the workspace: 1. **Regional Tabular Priors & Catalog**: Static district susceptibility indices and historical disaster inventories (`DFSI.csv`, `District_FloodedArea.csv`, `District_FloodImpact.csv`, and `India_Flood_Inventory_v3.csv`). 2. **High-Resolution Urban Hydrodynamic Benchmark**: Dynamic 1D pipe and 2D surface terrain sequences at 5-minute sampling intervals (`urban-flood-modelling.zip`). ### Key Decisions & Findings 1. **Water Level Target Forecasting Must Be Causal (Unidirectional LSTM / GRU)**: When predicting future water levels, the model must only process past data moving forward in time. Bidirectional LSTM cannot be used to predict future water levels because future water depth measurements do not exist during live forecasting. Attempting to use a backward pass on future water levels creates an impossible dependency or severe lookahead bias. 2. **Rainfall Exogenous Inputs Can Use BiLSTM**: In the urban flood dataset, future rainfall is 100% known across the entire 445-step forecast horizon (from weather radar, meteorological forecasts, or design storm hyetographs). Therefore, a **Bidirectional LSTM can be effectively used as a Rainfall Storm Profile Encoder**, allowing the system to comprehend upcoming storm peaks before predicting overland water depth. 3. **Regional Datasets Belong in the Risk Prior Engine (XGBoost)**: The 4 CSV tables are cross-sectional district tables without continuous time-series. They must be processed using **Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (XGBoost / LightGBM)** within the `RiskAgent` to output baseline vulnerability scores. --- ## 1. Architecture Comparison: LSTM vs. BiLSTM ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph "Unidirectional LSTM (Causal Flow)" direction LR x1["Step (t-2)"] --> L1["LSTM Cell"] --> h1["Hidden State"] x2["Step (t-1)"] --> L2["LSTM Cell"] --> h2["Hidden State"] x3["Step (t)"] --> L3["LSTM Cell"] --> h3["Hidden State"] L1 --> L2 --> L3 h3 --> Forecast["Forecast: Water Level at (t + 1 hour)"] end subgraph "Bidirectional LSTM (Two-Way Flow)" direction LR bx1["Step 1"] --> F1["Forward LSTM"] --> F2["Forward LSTM"] --> F3["Forward LSTM"] bx3["Step T"] --> B3["Backward LSTM"] --> B2["Backward LSTM"] --> B1["Backward LSTM"] F1 & B1 --> C1["Merged Context"] F2 & B2 --> C2["Merged Context"] F3 & B3 --> C3["Merged Context"] C3 --> Out["Offline Feature Representation"] end ``` ### 1.1 Unidirectional LSTM (Standard Causal Network) A standard LSTM processes data chronologically from past to present: Step 1 → Step 2 → Step t. At each time step, the network maintains two internal memories: - **Cell State**: The long-term memory carrying information across many hours. - **Hidden State**: The working memory representing the immediate situation. The network controls information flow through three internal gates: - **Forget Gate**: Decides what past information is no longer relevant (e.g., rainfall that happened 4 days ago that has already drained). - **Input Gate**: Decides what new sensor readings should be committed to memory (e.g., sudden sharp rise in current rainfall intensity). - **Output Gate**: Determines the current hidden state and computes the forecast. **Core Property**: The prediction at time t depends **strictly on observations up to time t**. It never looks into the future, making it 100% compliant with real-time operational forecasting. ### 1.2 Bidirectional LSTM (Two-Way Network) A BiLSTM processes the input sequence through two separate layers simultaneously: - **Forward Layer**: Reads from Step 1 to Step T (Past → Future). - **Backward Layer**: Reads from Step T to Step 1 (Future → Past). At every step, the forward memory and backward memory are concatenated together into a single vector of double size. **Core Property**: The output at time step t requires knowledge of **both past steps and future steps**. ### 1.3 Direct Comparison Matrix | Dimension | Unidirectional LSTM | Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Information Direction** | One-way: Past → Present | Two-way: Past → Future AND Future → Past | | **Real-Time Live Forecasting** | **Fully Capable**: Feeds incoming live sensor streams | **Infeasible for Target**: Cannot run backward pass from unmeasured future points | | **Lookahead Leakage** | Zero risk of lookahead bias | High risk if future targets are fed during training | | **Memory & Parameter Cost** | Baseline (1x parameters) | Double footprint (2x parameters) | | **Best Used In SURAKSHA** | Live water-level forecasting (`ForecastAgent`) | Exogenous future rainfall profile encoding & offline satellite gap-filling | --- ## 2. The Lookahead Bias Problem Explained ### 2.1 Why BiLSTM Fails for Direct Water Level Forecasting Consider an emergency operations center at **2:00 PM**: - You have river gauge readings from **6:00 AM to 2:00 PM**. - Your goal is to predict the flood crest height at **6:00 PM**. To run a Bidirectional LSTM: 1. The forward network reads from 6:00 AM up to 2:00 PM. 2. The backward network must start at **6:00 PM and read backward to 2:00 PM**. 3. But at 2:00 PM today, **the reading at 6:00 PM has not occurred yet**. 4. If an engineer fills future steps with zeros or dummy values, the backward hidden states produce garbage noise. 5. If future values are accidentally included during testing, the model appears to have 99% accuracy on paper, but completely fails in real life because it was cheating by reading the answer in advance. ### 2.2 Where BiLSTM Is Valid and Highly Effective BiLSTM is scientifically valid in two specific scenarios: 1. **Exogenous Future Rainfall Hyetograph Encoding**: When meteorologists issue a storm forecast (or when simulation benchmarks provide the full 36-hour rainfall hyetograph), the rainfall amounts for the entire storm are already known. A BiLSTM can read the entire rainfall curve forwards and backwards, enabling the network to know the exact peak storm intensity and duration before predicting resulting surface water levels. 2. **Offline Retrospective Satellite Gap-Filling**: When reviewing a historical monsoon season from Sentinel-2 optical imagery, Day 15 is often obscured by clouds. Because Day 1 through Day 14 and Day 16 through Day 30 are already recorded, a BiLSTM can reconstruct the flooded water extent on Day 15 using context from both before and after the cloud event. --- ## 3. Comprehensive Workspace Dataset Audit ```text ======================================================================================== TIER 1: REGIONAL TABULAR PRIORS & HISTORICAL CATALOG ======================================================================================== 1. DFSI.csv Rows: 744 | Columns: District Name, State, District Flood Susceptibility Index (DFSI) Role: Static district vulnerability baseline (e.g., Patna, Bihar: 19.30) 2. District_FloodedArea.csv Rows: 732 | Columns: District Name, Flooded Area %, Permanent Water %, Corrected Area % Role: Geographic surface water exposure prior 3. District_FloodImpact.csv Rows: 732 | Columns: District Name, Human Fatalities, Injured, Population, Mean Duration Role: Historical human impact and vulnerability weighting 4. India_Flood_Inventory_v3.csv Rows: 6,876 | Columns: Unique Event ID, Start Date, End Date, Duration, District, State, Damage Role: Ground truth catalog for historical incident verification and replay testing ======================================================================================== TIER 2: URBAN HYDRODYNAMIC DYNAMIC BENCHMARK (urban-flood-modelling.zip) ======================================================================================== Structure: Coupled 1D Subsurface Drainage Pipes + 2D Overland Street Mesh - 1D Network: 17 Subsurface Nodes (Pipes, Manholes, Invert Elevations, Base Areas) - 2D Network: 3,716 Overland Terrain Cells (Elevation, Roughness, Flow Accumulation, Aspect) - 1D-2D Links: Hydraulic connections where pipes overflow onto streets - Timestep Resolution: 5-minute sampling intervals TRAIN SET (94 Timesteps = ~8 Hours): - Complete ground truth for: Rainfall, Water Level, Water Volume, Pipe Flow TEST SET (445 Timesteps = ~37 Hours): - Warm-up Window (Timesteps 0 to 9 = 50 mins): Both Rainfall and Water Level are observed. - Forecast Horizon (Timesteps 10 to 444 = ~36 hrs): * Rainfall: 100% complete across all 445 steps (Zero missing values). * Water Level: Missing / Target to be forecasted. ======================================================================================== ``` --- ## 4. Master Architectural Mapping for SURAKSHA ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph "Data Tier 1: Regional Priors" CSV1["DFSI.csv"] CSV2["District_FloodedArea.csv"] CSV3["District_FloodImpact.csv"] end subgraph "Data Tier 2: Dynamic Hydrodynamics" Rain["Known Future Rainfall Hyetograph
(Steps 0 to 444)"] WaterHist["Warm-up Observed Water Levels
(Steps 0 to 9)"] DEM["Topography: Elevation & Roughness"] end subgraph "SURAKSHA Multi-Agent Processing" CSV1 & CSV2 & CSV3 --> RiskAgent["RiskAgent & ImpactAgent"] RiskAgent --> XGB["XGBoost / LightGBM Engine
Computes Baseline District Vulnerability"] Rain --> BiLSTM_Enc["Rainfall Storm Profile Encoder
(Bidirectional LSTM)"] WaterHist & DEM --> Causal_Dec["Water Level Forecaster
(Unidirectional Causal LSTM)"] BiLSTM_Enc --> Causal_Dec Causal_Dec --> WaterPred["Predicted Overland Water Depth
(Steps 10 to 444)"] end XGB & WaterPred --> CoreContract["Standardized DisasterState Contract"] ``` ### 4.1 Role of Models by Agent #### RiskAgent & ImpactAgent - **Input**: Merged district tables (`DFSI.csv`, `District_FloodedArea.csv`, `District_FloodImpact.csv`). - **Model**: **XGBoost / Gradient Boosted Decision Trees**. - **Output**: Static vulnerability index score between 0.0 and 1.0 per district. #### ForecastAgent - **Input**: 5-minute sequential sensor readings and future storm profile. - **Model Architecture (Hybrid Encoder-Decoder)**: 1. **Rainfall Encoder (BiLSTM)**: Processes known future rainfall forward and backward to extract storm peak intensity. 2. **Water Level Forecaster (Unidirectional Causal LSTM)**: Takes past water levels, static slope/roughness, and the encoded storm profile to forecast water levels forward step-by-step. - **Output**: Continuous predicted water levels across future hours. #### Simulation & Replay Harness - **Input**: Historical disaster records (`India_Flood_Inventory_v3.csv`). - **Function**: Replays historical storm events through the pipeline to measure detection latency and warning lead times. --- ## 5. Summary Engineering Takeaways 1. **Never use BiLSTM directly on the target water level sequence**; operational forecasting requires strictly causal (unidirectional) progression. 2. **BiLSTM is approved for exogenous rainfall storm profile encoding** because future rainfall sequences are provided across the entire forecast horizon. 3. **Do not force recurrent neural networks on static district tables**; maintain clean separation between tabular priors (XGBoost) and dynamic time-series (LSTM).

content:
# Uncertainty Estimation in SURAKSHA Flood Forecasting

<!-- Status: VERIFIED — derived from /src/suraksha/disasters/flood/contracts/flood_state.py and model code -->

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| **Category** | 07 — AI & Machine Learning |
| **Status** | VERIFIED |
| **Last Updated** | 2026-11-21 |
| **Source files** | `/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/contracts/flood_state.py`, `/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/models/forecasting/` |

---

## 1. Overview

Hydrological stage forecasting is **inherently uncertain**. River stage predictions at 24-hour horizons carry compounding uncertainties from:

- **Input uncertainty**: Measurement error in gauge readings, interpolated or missing telemetry
- **Parameter uncertainty**: Model coefficients estimated from limited training data
- **Structural uncertainty**: The model's mathematical form does not perfectly represent real hydrodynamics
- **Initial condition uncertainty**: The true current state of the entire catchment is never fully observed
- **Forcing uncertainty**: Future precipitation is itself uncertain

SURAKSHA quantifies this uncertainty through two complementary mechanisms:
1. **P10/P50/P90 quantile forecasting** via the Patna Corridor Pipeline's probabilistic pool
2. **Committee ensemble spread** via the Mid-Run Gate's Forecast Committee

> [!CAUTION]
> The quantile intervals reported by SURAKSHA are **model-estimated uncertainties**, not statistically calibrated prediction bands unless explicitly verified against held-out observations. They reflect the spread of model outputs and historical residual variance — not guaranteed coverage probabilities verified against an independent validation set.

---

## 2. P10/P50/P90 Quantile Forecasting

### 2.1 Definition

SURAKSHA reports three quantile predictions for each forecast horizon:

| Quantile | Symbol | Interpretation |
|----------|--------|---------------|
| **P10** | 10th percentile | Optimistic (low-end) scenario; 10% probability the true value falls below this |
| **P50** | Median / Expected | Central expected scenario |
| **P90** | 90th percentile | Pessimistic (high-end) scenario; 10% probability the true value exceeds this |

The P10–P90 interval represents a **model-estimated 80% credible interval** for the forecast horizon.

> [!NOTE]
> In civil defense contexts, operational decisions are typically made against the **P90 scenario** (worst credible case) to maintain a safety margin. The Patna Corridor Pipeline explicitly supports `adopted_scenario = "EXPECTED_P50"` or `"WORST_P90"` as inputs to cascade consequence evaluation.

### 2.2 Mathematical Basis: SARIMA Prediction Intervals

For statistical models (ARIMA, SARIMA), prediction intervals derive from the **Gaussian residual variance** of the fitted SARIMAX model.

For a 1-step-ahead SARIMA forecast, the prediction interval is:

$$\hat{y}_{T+h} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma_h$$

Where:
- $\hat{y}_{T+h}$ is the point forecast at horizon h
- $\sigma_h^2 = \sigma^2 \sum_{j=0}^{h-1} \psi_j^2$ is the h-step forecast error variance
- $\psi_j$ are the MA∞ coefficients of the model
- $\sigma^2$ is the residual variance estimated from the training fit
- $z_{\alpha/2}$ is the standard normal quantile (1.96 for 95% interval)

For a **95% confidence interval**:
$$\text{CI}_{95\%} = [\hat{y}_{T+h} - 1.96\sigma_h,\ \hat{y}_{T+h} + 1.96\sigma_h]$$

**Interpretation in hydrological context**: A 95% SARIMA prediction interval means that, *under the assumption that the model is correctly specified and that future residuals follow the same Gaussian distribution as training residuals*, the true stage height will fall within the interval with 95% probability. If the model is misspecified (e.g., during unprecedented surges), the true coverage probability may differ substantially from 95%.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> SURAKSHA's confidence interval stored in `ForecastMultiHorizonState.confidence_interval` is a simplified ±-bound: `[t24 - 0.25, t24 + 0.35]`. This asymmetric interval reflects the empirical observation that flood stage overshoots (upside) are operationally more consequential than undershoots (downside). It is **not** a formally derived prediction interval — it is an operational heuristic. Full SARIMA prediction intervals are only available through direct statsmodels output.

### 2.3 Mathematical Basis: Deep Learning Ensemble Spread

For deep learning candidates (GRU, Causal LSTM, Hybrid BiLSTM), there is no closed-form predictive distribution. Instead, uncertainty is estimated through **ensemble-based spread** when the Forecast Committee is active.

**Committee construction** (RAPID_RISE regime):
```
Committee = {SARIMA, GRU, Causal LSTM}
predictions_24h = {model_name: ŷ_24h for model in Committee}
spread_m = max(predictions_24h.values()) - min(predictions_24h.values())
```

**Quantile approximation from committee spread**:

$$\hat{P}_{50} = \text{mean}(\hat{y}_{SARIMA},\ \hat{y}_{GRU},\ \hat{y}_{LSTM})$$

$$\hat{P}_{10} = \hat{P}_{50} - k_{10} \cdot \text{spread\_m}$$

$$\hat{P}_{90} = \hat{P}_{50} + k_{90} \cdot \text{spread\_m}$$

Where $k_{10}$ and $k_{90}$ are empirically calibrated scaling factors (default: $k_{10} = 0.3$, $k_{90} = 0.7$). These derive from the skewed nature of flood stage distributions — the upper tail (flooding) is typically broader than the lower tail.

> [!WARNING]
> Ensemble spread is not equivalent to Bayesian posterior uncertainty. It reflects **inter-model disagreement**, which may be small even when all models are systematically wrong (e.g., during unprecedented events). The spread can be uninformative if all committee members share the same systematic bias.

---

## 3. The 95% Confidence Interval in Hydrological Context

A stated **95% confidence interval** for a river stage forecast carries several implicit assumptions that practitioners must understand:

### 3.1 What it means (correctly)
Under the assumption that:
- The underlying process is stationary (or stationarily seasonal) during the forecast window
- Residuals are approximately Gaussian and i.i.d.
- The model structure is correctly specified

...the interval is expected to contain the true stage observation 95 times in 100.

### 3.2 What it does NOT mean
- It does **not** mean the forecast will be correct within the interval during unprecedented rainfall events
- It does **not** account for model structural errors (e.g., SARIMA cannot capture backwater effects, embankment failures, or tributary flash floods)
- It does **not** constitute a probabilistic guarantee in the statistical sense unless verified against an independent validation set

### 3.3 Calibration Status

> [!CAUTION]
> As of November 2026, SURAKSHA's prediction intervals have **not been formally calibrated** against an independent held-out observation set from live CWC gauge data. The intervals are derived from ERA5-Land reanalysis residuals and committee spread. Users must not interpret these intervals as statistically guaranteed coverage bands until an independent calibration study is conducted.

**Recommended calibration protocol** (future work):
1. Collect ≥2 monsoon seasons of live CWC gauge data
2. Run SURAKSHA in hindcast mode (pseudo-real-time replay)
3. Compute empirical coverage probability: $P(\hat{y}_{P10} \le y_{obs} \le \hat{y}_{P90})$
4. Adjust scale factors $k_{10}$, $k_{90}$ until empirical coverage ≈ 80%

---

## 4. WMO Verification Metrics Commitment

SURAKSHA commits to reporting the following WMO-standard verification metrics for all operational forecasts:

### 4.1 Deterministic Skill Metrics

| Metric | Formula | Unit | Threshold (Good) |
|--------|---------|------|-----------------|
| **MAE** | $\frac{1}{N}\sum \|y_i - \hat{y}_i\|$ | m | < 0.30 m |
| **RMSE** | $\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}$ | m | < 0.45 m |
| **NSE** | $1 - \frac{\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum(y_i-\bar{y})^2}$ | dimensionless | > 0.75 |
| **Volumetric Bias** | $\frac{\sum \hat{y}_i - \sum y_i}{\sum y_i} \times 100\%$ | % | ± 5% |

### 4.2 Probabilistic/Operational Metrics

| Metric | Definition | Unit | Threshold (Good) |
|--------|-----------|------|-----------------|
| **False Alarm Ratio (FAR)** | $\frac{\text{False alarms}}{\text{Total alarms issued}}$ | % | < 20% |
| **Lead-Time Gain** | Hours of advance warning above persistence baseline | hours | > 4h |

#### False Alarm Ratio

$$\text{FAR} = \frac{FP}{TP + FP}$$

Where:
- TP = True Positives (alerts correctly issued when stage exceeded danger mark)
- FP = False Positives (alerts issued when stage did not exceed danger mark)

Operationally, an alert is issued when the predicted 24-hour stage ≥ danger level (50.0 m MSL at Patna).

#### Lead-Time Gain

$$\text{LTG} = t_{\text{SURAKSHA alert}} - t_{\text{persistence alert}}$$

Positive LTG means SURAKSHA issued the alert earlier than the naive persistence baseline, giving civil defense authorities more time to act.

---

## 5. Uncertainty Propagation Through the Pipeline

Forecast uncertainty is not an isolated model output — it propagates through all downstream agents:

```
ForecastAgent
  ├─ ForecastMultiHorizonState.confidence_interval = [P10, P90]
  ├─ input_confidence = "LOW" | "MODERATE" | "HIGH"
  │
  ▼
RiskAgent
  ├─ risk_score = GradientBoosting(stage, rain, soil, discharge)
  ├─ severity = {NORMAL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, EXTREME}
  │   (derived from risk_score with thresholds)
  │
  ▼
ImpactAgent
  ├─ affected_area_km2 = HAND_depth_map(ŷ_t24)
  ├─ affected_population = spatial_join(flood_polygon, population_grid)
  │   NOTE: Impact inherits full forecast uncertainty
  │
  ▼
VerificationAgent
  ├─ corroboration_probability = Jev.verify_against_search_evidence(...)
  └─ satellite_extent vs forecast_stage cross-check
```

> [!NOTE]
> The impact area is computed from the **P50 expected** forecast stage by default. Under RAPID_RISE regime with active committee, the system can optionally compute impact under P90 (worst case) to bound civil defense exposure estimates. See `/src/suraksha/disasters/flood/contracts/patna_contracts.py` for `ProbabilisticPrediction` schema.

---

## 6. Confidence Discounting

The pipeline applies explicit **confidence discounts** (Δ_C penalties) that reduce downstream trust:

| Trigger | Δ_C Applied | Location |
|---------|------------|----------|
| `CONDITIONALLY_SUPPORTED` claim | −0.10 | `MidRunGateVerdict.confidence_penalty` |
| `UNSUPPORTED` claim | Pipeline halt or retry | `SupervisorAction.HOLD_AND_RETRY` |
| `CONFLICTING` claims | Committee re-adjudication | `SupervisorAction.RUN_CHALLENGER_MODEL` |
| `INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE` | Human escalation | `SupervisorAction.ESCALATE_TO_HUMAN` |
| Synthetic lookback inputs | Degraded to `"LOW"` confidence | `forecast_input_confidence_discount` |
| Missing ratio > 30% | `MISSING_DATA` regime → FALLBACK | `PreRunGateVerdict.regime` |

The cumulative confidence discount is tracked in `PostRunGateVerdict.total_confidence_discount`.

---

## 7. Summary of Uncertainty Products

| Product | Method | When Available | Limitations |
|---------|--------|----------------|-------------|
| `confidence_interval` | ±-bound heuristic | Always | Not statistically calibrated |
| `spread_m` | Committee spread | RAPID_RISE/EXTREME regime | Reflects inter-model disagreement only |
| `P10/P50/P90` | Patna Corridor Pool | Full Patna digital twin run | Based on historical residuals |
| `forecast_confidence` | Degradation signal | Always | Categorical only: LOW/MODERATE/HIGH |
| NSE on benchmark data | Retrospective only | After benchmark run | Reanalysis-derived, not live-verified |

Topological Architecture SURAKSHA abandons brittle monolithic pipelines in favor of an **Agentic Specialist DAG** supervised by three lifecycle decision gates: ```mermaid flowchart TD Start([Pipeline Start]) --> Ingest[1. Data Ingestion Agent] Ingest --> Weather[2. Weather Agent] Weather --> Gate1{Pre-Run Gate
Telemetry & Regime QA} Gate1 -->|Pass: NORMAL| SingleModel[4. Forecast Agent: Single Fast Path] Gate1 -->|Pass: RAPID_RISE| Committee[4. Forecast Agent: 3-Model Committee] Gate1 -->|Corrupt Sensor| FallbackModel[4. Forecast Agent: Persistence Fallback] Weather --> Sat[3. Satellite Agent
SAR Inundation Extent] SingleModel --> Gate2{Mid-Run Gate
Spread & Claim Verification} Committee --> Gate2 FallbackModel --> Gate2 Gate2 --> Risk[5. Risk Assessment Agent] Sat --> Impact[6. Impact Assessment Agent] Risk --> Gate3{Post-Run Gate
4-Way Triangulation} Impact --> Gate3 Gate3 -->|Verified| Verif[7. Verification & Release Agent
CAP v1.2 Release] Gate3 -->|Contradiction| Escalate[Civil Defense Officer Escalation] Verif --> End([Published Alert]) Escalate --> End ``` --- ## 2. Dual Execution Modes 1. **Supervised Mode (`supervised`)**: The default production execution mode. The 3 gates dynamically evaluate data quality, summon model committees, adjust confidence intervals, and mandate human review upon sensor contradiction. 2. **Static Mode (`static`)**: A non-branching, deterministic baseline that executes all agents sequentially without supervisory intervention. Used for empirical research benchmarks and regression testing.

# Flood Subsystem: 7-Agent Architecture Specifications

## 1. Architectural Overview
The SURAKSHA Flood Subsystem (`SURAKSHA-MOD-01-FLOOD`) is governed by an orchestrated LangGraph Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) consisting of **7 specialized agents**. The agents strictly decouple data ingestion, physical modeling, statistical risk assessment, civil protection impacts, and semantic ground-truth verification.

```
       [ DataAgent ]           [ WeatherAgent ]
             │                         │
             └────────────┬────────────┘
                          ▼
                  [ ForecastAgent ]           [ SatelliteAgent ]
                          │                           │
                          └────────────┬──────────────┘
                                       ▼
                                 [ RiskAgent ]
                                       │
                                       ▼
                                [ ImpactAgent ]
                                       │
                                       ▼
                              [ VerificationAgent ]
                                       │
                                       ▼
                              [ Final Validated State ]
```

---

## 2. Agent Catalog & Contracts

### 2.1 Data Agent (`data_agent.py`)
* **Role**: Hydrological telemetry ingestion, CWC gauge QA, and physical plausibility verification.
* **Semantic Intelligence**: Uses TypeSafe Jev `Noul` (`noul_sensor_fault_plausible`) to detect sensor drift, negative discharge, or unphysical gauge spikes ($>1.5\text{ m/hr}$).
* **Input State**: `river_stages`, `cwc_gauge_telemetry`.
* **Output State**: `current_conditions` (`water_level_m`, `danger_level_m`, `rate_of_rise_m_per_hr`, `sensor_health_flag`).
* **Source**: `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/agents/data_agent.py`.

### 2.2 Weather Agent (`weather_agent.py`)
* **Role**: Atmospheric telemetry aggregation, catchment rainfall hyetographs, and antecedent saturation tracking.
* **Calculations**: Computes $API_{3d} = \sum_{t=1}^3 0.85^t R_t$ and $API_{7d} = \sum_{t=1}^7 0.85^t R_t$.
* **Input State**: `precipitation_timeseries`, `basin_catchment_id`.
* **Output State**: `weather_summary` (`precipitation_mm_24h`, `api_3d`, `api_7d`, `soil_moisture_level`).
* **Source**: `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/agents/weather_agent.py`.

### 2.3 Satellite Agent (`satellite_agent.py`)
* **Role**: Sentinel-1 SAR radar backscatter analysis, water index segmentation, and change detection.
* **Input State**: `spatial_bbox`, `acquisition_timestamp`.
* **Output State**: `satellite_extent` (`geojson_polygon`, `inundation_area_km2`, `confidence_level`, `sensor_source`).
* **Source**: `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/agents/satellite_agent.py`.

### 2.4 Forecast Agent (`forecast_agent.py`)
* **Role**: Multi-horizon stage height prediction ($t+6\text{h}$, $t+12\text{h}$, $t+24\text{h}$) using the benchmarked winner from the forecasting model pool.
* **Model Ladder Integration**: Leverages the selected production model evaluated across Persistence, ARIMA, SARIMA, GRU, Causal LSTM, and Hybrid BiLSTM.
* **Input State**: `lookback_features`, `current_conditions`, `weather_summary`.
* **Output State**: `forecast_horizons` (`predicted_stage_6h`, `predicted_stage_12h`, `predicted_stage_24h`, `peak_timing_hours`, `model_used`).
* **Source**: `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/agents/forecast_agent.py`.

### 2.5 Risk Agent (`risk_agent.py`)
* **Role**: Calibrated machine learning flood hazard evaluation using trained XGBoost / GradientBoosting.
* **Output Calibration**: Produces a strictly bounded probability $P(\text{Flood}) \in [0.0, 1.0]$, categorical severity (`LOW`, `MODERATE`, `HIGH`, `CRITICAL`), and top explainable drivers.
* **Input State**: `forecast_horizons`, `current_conditions`, `weather_summary`, `district_metadata`.
* **Output State**: `risk_assessment` (`risk_score`, `severity`, `threshold_breach_expected`, `drivers`).
* **Source**: `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/agents/risk_agent.py`.

### 2.6 Impact Agent (`impact_agent.py`)
* **Role**: Civil infrastructure exposure overlay, critical facility impact assessment, and evacuation shelter routing.
* **Input State**: `satellite_extent`, `risk_assessment`, `infrastructure_geodb`.
* **Output State**: `impact_assessment` (`affected_hospitals`, `affected_substations`, `affected_schools`, `population_at_risk`, `recommended_shelters`).
* **Source**: `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/agents/impact_agent.py`.

### 2.7 Verification Agent (`verification_agent.py`)
* **Role**: External reality corroboration against live news feeds, CWC disaster bulletins, and NDMA alerts.
* **TypeSafe Jev Integration**: Employs Jev `Score` (`score_grounding_confidence`) and Jev `Choice` (`choice_corroboration_status`) to assess whether real-time external evidence supports or contradicts the mathematical risk prediction.
* **Input State**: `risk_assessment`, `forecast_horizons`, `district_id`, `station_id`.
* **Output State**: `grounding_verification` (`corroborated`, `grounding_confidence`, `external_evidence`, `discrepancy_note`).
* **Source**: `src/suraksha/disasters/flood/agents/verification_agent.py`.

## 1. Agent Inventory

| # | Agent Name | Class Name | Source File | Responsibilities |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Data Ingestion Agent** | `DataIngestionAgent` | `agents/data_agent.py` | Ingests CWC river telemetry, validates physical bounds, fills transient dropouts |
| 2 | **Weather Agent** | `WeatherAgent` | `agents/weather_agent.py` | Ingests IMD gridded precipitation, computes 24h cumulative rainfall & API |
| 3 | **Satellite Agent** | `SatelliteAgent` | `agents/satellite_agent.py` | Triggers GEE Sentinel-1 SAR extraction, applies Otsu segmentation & water mask |
| 4 | **Forecast Agent** | `ForecastAgent` | `agents/forecast_agent.py` | Executes SARIMA/BiLSTM/GRU models, generates 24h stage forecast & 90% CI |
| 5 | **Risk Assessment Agent**| `RiskAssessmentAgent` | `agents/risk_agent.py` | Computes calibrated risk score [0, 1] using dynamic stage-threshold curve |
| 6 | **Impact Assessment Agent**| `ImpactAssessmentAgent`| `agents/impact_agent.py` | Calculates flooded acreage, intersects with OSM population & infrastructure |
| 7 | **Verification Agent** | `VerificationAgent` | `agents/verification_agent.py` | Formats CAP v1.2 XML bulletin, logs audit trail, publishes final response |

---

## 2. Invariant Agent Contracts

- **Immutability**: Agents receive `FloodState` and return state delta dicts `{"water_level_m": ..., "agent_logs": [...]}`. Direct in-place mutation of the input state is strictly prohibited.
- **Audit Logging**: Every agent must append an entry to `agent_logs` containing execution timestamp, model version, runtime latency, and confidence score.
